Appendix C: Codes of Practice and Legislation

Bill teams should read this section if there is a proposal to adopt, use, or otherwise refer to a code of practice or similar document in implementing the legislation. Where it is proposed to introduce a code of practice in a way or for a purpose which departs from the guidance below, Ministers should be aware that this is likely to be controversial, particularly in the House of Lords.

Where use of a code of practice is contemplated as part of, or as an adjunct to, the scheme of an Act, the drafting of the code ought to begin early enough to enable a decision as to whether statutory provision is required, and if so what kind of provision is appropriate, to be made with a clear idea of the proposed contents of the code. Equally, if Parliament is to be asked to enact statutory provisions relating to a code, a draft of the proposed code should if at all possible be made available so that the appropriateness of the statutory provisions can be properly considered.

Failure to do this can hinder the passage of the enabling legislation. While this chapter offers a general guide only and the paramount consideration in every case must be the framing of a legislative scheme which is appropriate for the particular purpose in hand, departure from the general rules in this guidance should rarely be necessary and will require justification. In particular, departments should bear in mind that any unusual or novel provision will be closely scrutinised in Parliament.

Meaning of ‘code of practice’

A ‘code of practice’ is an authoritative statement of practice to be followed in some field. It typically differs from legislation in that it offers guidance rather than imposing requirements: its prescriptions are not hard and fast rules but guidelines which may allow considerable latitude in their practical application and may be departed from in appropriate circumstances. The provisions of a code are not directly enforceable by legal proceedings, which is not to say that they may not have significant legal effects. A code of practice, unlike a legislative text, may also contain explanatory material and argument.

A number of different kinds of document may be described by statute as a ‘code of practice’. They may contain general principles or minute technical details, they may describe existing practice or practice which is recommended for the future and they may contain explanation and information of various kinds. Conversely, other terms may be used to describe essentially the same kind of document. This guidance refers to ‘codes of practice’ but its comments apply equally to similar documents under other names.

It will usually be undesirable for an Act to refer to some other kind of document as a ‘code of practice’. This is apt to mislead as to the status or intention of the document. Some more accurate descriptive title should be used.

Different kinds of provisions may be found within a single document. Accordingly, where this guidance refers to a type of code the comment should be read as applicable to particular provisions of that description in a code of practice.

Is statutory provision necessary?

This guidance is concerned with legislation and is therefore not concerned with non-statutory codes. However, a preliminary question which must always be considered is whether statutory provision is necessary.

There are many things departments can properly do without express statutory authority. It has been the practice for many years for departments to issue information, advice or exhortation of various kinds, for the guidance of the public or of the authorities or officers charged with administering some branch of Government. These documents may be described as ‘codes’ and may be of considerable practical importance. It does not follow that statutory provision is necessary.

A provision which merely confers on a Minister power to issue a code of practice consisting of information, advice or exhortation which is not intended to have any particular legal effect is unnecessary.

Statutory provision is justifiable if the code is intended to have a particular legal effect (the various types of which are described below). It is also justifiable if it is intended to impose a legal duty to issue a code of practice or to impose legal requirements as to the procedure to be followed in connection with its issue. Either of those courses indicates that importance is attached to the code of practice and careful consideration should be given to the question of its legal effect.

Statutory provision may also be justifiable when setting up a statutory body to make clear that the body has power to issue codes of practice. Express provision is not necessary where, as will usually be the case, the issuing of codes is merely incidental to the body’s general functions.

If statutory provision is necessary but the code is not intended to have any particular legal effect of the descriptions below, there should be appropriate words indicating that the code is issued only for purposes of advice or information.

Codes of practice are not to be used to define specific legal obligations. Where specific legal obligations are to be imposed, breach of which leads directly to civil or criminal liability, their content should be spelled out in primary or secondary legislation. A code of practice is not appropriate for this purpose, either to delineate the main obligation or to provide for exceptions or defences.

A code of practice may be appropriate to explain or supplement the provisions of primary or secondary legislation. It should not be regarded as a substitute for legislation. It is the function of legislation to set minimum standards of conduct and it is usual to provide for penalties for those who fall below the minimum standard and for legal remedies for the protection or compensation of those who suffer injury or loss as a result. It is usual to set legal minimum standards notwithstanding that the overall policy objective is to raise standards generally above the minimum - an objective towards which a code of practice may contribute.

Codes addressed to the public or a section of it: failure to comply with code as evidence of breach of legal duty The most common type of provision giving legal effect to a code of practice is that making failure to comply with the code evidence of breach of some more general legal duty. The codes in relation to which such provision is made are normally addressed to the public at large or a section of it (for instance, road users or employers).

The liability is not for breach of the code but for breach of a duty arising elsewhere.

There is no essential difference between the two styles of provision to this effect. The first type of provision focuses on the effect of breach or compliance in establishing liability; the second focuses on the effect of the code’s provisions in elaborating standards of conduct. Both types of provision produce substantially the same result: that in certain kinds of proceedings the code is an element in deciding the issue of liability or some other question, but is not itself decisive.

In neither case does the provision directly shift the legal or evidential burden of proof. The significance of a failure to comply with a provision of a code cannot be assessed except in relation to the circumstances of a particular case. The evidential weight depends on the relevance and importance of the failure in relation to the matters to be proved in order to establish liability.

When considering what evidential effect should be attributed to any particular code careful consideration should be given to identifying so far as possible what proceedings, and what issues, a breach of the code may be relevant to. The resulting statutory provision should be as specific as is possible.

In general the first type of provision is preferable because it is more specific, but it cannot be regarded as universally applicable. It may be that some adaptation of it, or something more akin to the "questions arising" form, is in particular circumstances more appropriate. For instance, it may not be "liability" which is in issue but some other question; and the proceedings may not be ordinary legal proceedings.

A form appropriate to the determination of issues in legal proceedings should not be stretched to cover the exercise of administrative functions which is more aptly dealt with by a duty to have regard. It may in some cases be necessary to provide for both types of effect in relation to the same code.

There is a variant form of the evidential code provision in s.17 (1) and (2) of the Health & Safety at Work Act 1974 (c.37) which expressly shifts the burden of proof. It is not usual to attempt in legislation to modify the operation of general legal principles such as those relating to the evidential burden of proof whose impact in the nature of things varies from case to case. And to shift the legal (or "persuasive") burden of proof would normally be regarded as giving a code too much legal force. For these reasons, although this provision may be justified in its particular context, it should not in general be regarded as a precedent for future legislation.

Codes addressed to authorities and officers: duty to have regard to code

Another type of code of practice is that relevant to the exercise of statutory functions by public authorities or officers.

General principles of administrative law require public authorities or officers in exercising their functions to direct themselves properly and to take into account all relevant factors and not to take into account irrelevant factors. Failure to do so may result in a decision or other Act being challenged in proceedings for judicial review or simply being regarded as being legally ineffective.

If the provisions of a code are intended to be included among the relevant factors in the exercise of a class of functions it will normally be desirable to make this clear by requiring the relevant authorities to have regard to the code, or, which amounts to the same thing, to take it into account. As indicated above, the consequences of their failing to do so are governed by general administrative law; ad hoc statutory provision as to the effect of failure is neither necessary nor desirable.

The requirement that an authority or officer must have regard to the code means that the authority or officer must consider the provisions of the code and give them due weight in coming to their decision. They are not bound to follow the code if they properly conclude that the recommendations of the code are, in a particular case, either not relevant or are outweighed by other considerations.

Careful consideration should be given to identifying the persons or authorities who are required to have regard to the code and the decisions or functions in relation to which the provisions of the code are to be taken into account. Again, the statutory provision should be as specific as the circumstances admit.

Codes administered by authorities having regulatory or disciplinary powers: failure to comply with code leading to action by authority

Another form of provision found is that failure to comply with the provisions of a code of practice is a ground for the exercise of regulatory or disciplinary powers by some supervisory authority or, which amounts to the same thing, that an authority shall exercise its general supervisory powers so as to secure compliance with the code. The code itself may be one issued by the authority in question, by Ministers or by some third party.

This type of provision will not normally offend against the principle mentioned above (that a code of practice should not to be used to define specific legal obligations) because any legal liability arises as a result of the exercise of the authority’s general powers and not simply from the failure to comply with the code. The authority will normally take action on some wider ground than breach of the code alone and will have a discretion as to how it exercises its regulatory powers.

The effect of a breach of the code is in such cases broadly similar to that mentioned above in that it is a ground on which a sanction may, but need not, be imposed. However, similar considerations to those mentioned above (that a code of practice should not to be used to define specific legal obligations) apply if what is envisaged is a set of binding rules breach of which will, without anything else having to be shown or otherwise required, lead directly to the imposition of a sanction.

Statutory mention of codes having extra statutory effect

The framing of codes of practice by trade associations, professional bodies and other self- regulatory organisations is commonplace and whatever legal effect they have is basically a matter of private law. There are a number of statutory provisions which confer duties on regulatory authorities to encourage the preparation and dissemination of codes by non-governmental bodies.

These provisions do not confer any additional legal effect on the codes in question.

Drafting codes of practice

Codes of practice are drawn up for a wide range of audiences and purposes and contain a variety of provisions. No general guidance is possible, or indeed necessary, as to the manner in which a code is expressed. The main purpose of a code of practice is to inform and guide and it will fail in that object if its provisions are not clear.

Every code which is drawn up under statutory authority should refer to its authorising provision and recite or summarise the purposes for which it is issued.

Where a code is to have legal effect of any of the kinds mentioned above, it should also recite or summarise the provisions giving it that legal effect. Such a code must also be sufficiently precisely drafted for its intended purpose. In particular, where a code contains provisions of different kinds it should be arranged, so far as practicable, in such a way as to make it clear which passages are prescriptive and which contain only exhortation, explanation or information.

Where use of a code of practice is contemplated as part of, or as an adjunct to, the scheme of an Act, the drafting of the code ought to begin early enough to enable a decision as to whether statutory provision is required, and if so what kind of provision is appropriate, to be made with a clear idea of the proposed contents of the code. Equally, if Parliament is to be asked to enact statutory provisions relating to a code, a draft of the proposed code should if at all possible be made available so that the appropriateness of the statutory provisions can be properly considered.

Failure to do this can hinder the passage of the enabling legislation.

Parliamentary procedure for codes of practice

Departments should ensure that there is appropriate provision for Parliamentary procedure where the nature and importance of the subject matter of a code warrants it. In the case of evidential codes (where the failure to comply with a code can be taken as evidence of breach of legal duty) and codes to which authorities are to have regard, there is a presumption in favour of parliamentary procedure of some kind; but this may not be appropriate for detailed technical documents. If it is envisaged that a code will be frequently amended, it may be sufficient to provide for parliamentary procedure only in relation to its original issue or revocation.

The considerations involved in deciding between affirmative and negative procedure, or no procedure, are broadly similar to those applicable in the case of subordinate legislation. Parliament will wish to consider the substance of the code, so that provision for Parliamentary procedure should relate to the code itself and not, where there is one, to the order bringing the code into operation, even though that may be a statutory instrument. In the case of the approval by Ministers of a code drawn up by a third party it may be appropriate to provide for Parliamentary procedure in relation to the approval order, the code itself having been laid before Parliament.

Publication and commencement

Departments should ensure that there are satisfactory arrangements for publication or other means of bringing the contents of a code of practice to the notice of those to whom it is directed.

No special statutory provision is required, although it is sometimes found, for the publication and sale of codes. In the case of codes addressed to authorities or officers it should be borne in mind that others will have a legitimate interest in the contents of the code, for instance, in order to challenge a decision taken in breach of the code. In such cases other means of disseminating the necessary information may be appropriate, for instance, publishing the code on a website, as a circular in a series sold through TSO, or the department’s designated publisher including the code in a relevant annual report which is published. Every code issued under statutory authority ought to be made available to Parliament; if it is not otherwise available, by placing a copy in the Library of each House.

It will often be important to know when a code, or an amendment of it, came into operation. There is no reason why this should not be stated in the code itself but it may be convenient to make provision in a separate order, particularly where it is necessary to include transitional provisions or savings. Where such orders are made by Ministers they should be made by statutory instrument.

Evidence: Admissibility and proof of document

Provision is sometimes found that a code of practice is to be "admissible" in certain kinds of legal proceedings. A code (whether expressed as a command or a statement of fact) is a statement of the opinion of the maker of the code as to what ought to be done. Such a statement would not normally be relevant to a court’s consideration of what is legally required to be done. That may be simply a matter of law on which the court makes up its own mind after hearing argument; or it may involve questions of fact (such as, what is "best practicable means" or "reasonable care") on which expert witnesses may be called. The contents of a code of practice are a form of “opinion evidence” of someone who is not a witness and may not be an expert in the sense under discussion (i.e. the code of practice is compiled by persons who are unidentified and who if identified might not count as experts). To provide that the code is admissible, therefore, means that the document can be put before the court despite these general rules of the law of evidence.

Provision to this effect is unnecessary if the court is directed by the Act to take the code into account for some specified purpose. It must follow from such a duty that the court can look at the code whatever its status may be so far as the general rules of evidence are concerned.

This question must be distinguished from the question of how the text of the code is proved. Assuming a code of practice is "admissible" or may be relied on in particular proceedings, there may in some cases be technical difficulties in proving that the document is in fact the code referred to in the Act or in establishing what the text of the code is. In criminal proceedings, in particular, the prosecution may find itself put to proof of a code not in common use or there may be a real dispute as to the correct text of a code at any material time. As well as the text, the party relying on a code may be required to prove when the code, or an amendment, was issued or came into operation.

Codes and related documents issued by Government departments may have the benefit of the Documentary Evidence Act 1868 (c.37), as amended and extended, which enables the document to be proved by a copy purporting to be printed by, or under the superintendence or authority of, His Majesty’s Stationery Office. In other cases it will be necessary to consider whether provision should be made for facilitating the proof of the document, and of any order or other instrument approving it for the purposes of the statute, by creating a presumption that such a document is what it purports to be.

Appendix D: Securing Legislative Consent Motions in the Devolved Legislatures

General principles

In each of the devolved legislatures the process of securing a Legislative Consent Motion (LCM) begins with a legislative consent memorandum being tabled by the corresponding devolved government. This memorandum cannot be tabled until the Westminster bill has been introduced by the UK Government (UKG) before Parliament. The subsequent processes and timings vary slightly between the devolved legislatures as set out below. In theory, the LCM process can be expedited in all three of the devolved legislatures, however the timing and process of LCMs is very much a matter for the devolved legislatures to consider.

LCMs must be passed by the devolved legislatures before the bill reaches its final amending stages in the second House in Parliament[footnote 19]. This is to ensure that UKG has the contingency option of tabling amendments to the bill to remove or amend the relevant provisions/clauses in the event that any of the devolved legislatures choose to withhold legislative consent.

Further information on the LCM processes in each of the devolved legislatures can be found in Devolution Guidance Notes (DGNs) 8, 10 and 18.

Scottish Parliament

The Scottish Parliament’s Standing Orders set out how the devolved legislature deals with LCMs. The Standing Orders state that, once legislation is introduced in the UK Parliament, and if the legislation relates to a matter within the legislative competence of the Scottish Parliament (or alters/modifies executive or legislative competence), the Scottish Government is required to lodge a legislative consent memorandum within two weeks (although that can be extended if the Scottish Government can secure agreement from the Scottish Parliament to suspend the relevant Standing Order). This memorandum should set out the provisions which are considered to engage the LCM process alongside the Scottish Government’s recommendation on whether or not the Scottish Parliament should agree to give legislative consent.

Prior to the introduction of the memorandum, the Scottish Parliament’s Presiding Officer must determine whether the legislative consent memorandum falls within the scope of the Scottish Parliament’s Standing Orders in relation to LCMs.

When a memorandum has been tabled in the Scottish Parliament, the process can take around eight weeks and cannot be expedited without the agreement of the Scottish Parliament. As part of this process, the memorandum will be considered by a lead scrutiny committee of the Scottish Parliament, who will produce a report prior to a final vote on the LCM itself. In some cases, UKG Ministers may be asked to attend a committee session in order to provide formal evidence in relation to the bill.

Under the Scottish Parliament’s Standing Orders, it is possible for any Member of the Scottish Parliament (MSP) to table an LCM before the Scottish Parliament, however LCMs are almost always tabled and promoted by the Scottish Government.

Senedd Cymru/Welsh Parliament

Under the Senedd Cymru/Welsh Parliament’s Standing Orders for Westminster bills that engage the LCM process, the Welsh Government must lay a legislative consent memorandum in the Senedd setting out the provisions which fall within the legislative competence of the Senedd. The memorandum must identify “relevant provision” (ie: provisions which fall within the legislative competence of the Senedd or provisions which modify or alter the legislative or executive competence of the Senedd or Welsh Ministers), and explain whether or not the Welsh Government considers it appropriate for a Westminster bill to legislate in areas of devolved competence. The Senedd’s Standing Orders also state that such a memorandum must normally be laid no later than two weeks after the bill’s introduction in the Westminster Parliament.

The Senedd’s Business Committee normally refers the Welsh Government’s legislative consent memorandum to a Senedd committee for scrutiny and sets a date by when that committee must report back to the Senedd on it. In some cases, UKG Ministers may be asked to attend a committee session in order to provide formal evidence in relation to the bill. Once the committee has reported on the memorandum, or the deadline by which the committee is required to report has passed, any Member of the Senedd (in practice, usually a Welsh Minister) may table an LCM for the Senedd to consider and vote on.

Whilst there is no specific role for the Senedd’s Presiding Officer in relation to Westminster bills, their general competence to determine questions on the interpretation or application of the Standing Orders would enable them to rule out an LCM debate if the Welsh Government’s legislative consent memorandum fails to identify “relevant provision”, or if the process of scrutiny was defective.

The process from laying the memorandum to the date of the Senedd‘s LCM debate and vote usually takes around six to eight weeks, although this can depend on the complexity and content of the bill being considered for legislative consent.

Northern Ireland Assembly

The LCM process in the Northern Ireland Assembly begins with the relevant Northern Ireland Executive Minister laying a legislative consent memorandum before the Northern Ireland Assembly, either explaining that consent is being sought or explaining why the Minister is declining to recommend that consent be given. This cannot happen until after the bill has been introduced at Westminster and should normally happen within ten working days of the bill’s introduction at Westminster.

It is possible for any other Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) to lay a legislative consent memorandum. This may only happen after either the Northern Ireland Executive Minister has laid a legislative consent memorandum; or the Northern Ireland Executive Minister has laid a memorandum explaining why consent is not being recommended; or the ten working day period has elapsed.

Once a legislative consent memorandum has been laid before the Northern Ireland Assembly, those provisions of the bill dealing with a transferred matter are referred to the relevant Northern Ireland Assembly scrutiny committee for consideration, unless the Assembly orders otherwise. The committee may report its opinion to the Northern Ireland Assembly within 15 working days of referral.

At least five working days after publication of the committee’s report (or 20 working days after referral to the committee), the relevant Northern Ireland Executive Minister may then table an LCM and move the motion. The Northern Ireland Assembly will then vote on whether to agree to the LCM i.e. give consent. If the motion is not supported then consent will not have been provided.

Unique to Northern Ireland, a Petition of Concern can apply to any Northern Ireland Assembly vote, including a vote on an LCM. If 30 or more MLAs support a petition, then the vote requires either the support of a majority of the members voting, a majority of the designated Nationalists voting and a majority of the designated Unionists voting; or the support of 60 per cent of the members voting, 40 per cent of the designated Nationalists voting and 40 per cent of the designated Unionists voting. Except in exceptional circumstances a petition must be delivered to the Speaker at least one hour before the vote is due to take place; if one is presented, the vote cannot take place for a further 24 hours.

The LCM process in Northern Ireland (involving the agreement of the Northern Ireland Executive, the relevant committee scrutiny and vote of the Northern Ireland Assembly itself) can generally take around eight weeks. There is no urgent procedure in the Assembly’s Standing Orders, although Standing Orders can be suspended with the agreement of the Northern Ireland Assembly itself.

Appendix E: Delegated Legislation Toolkit

An Act of Parliament can give ministers or others the power (sometimes called a ‘delegated power’) to make secondary legislation. This toolkit will help you decide whether to include delegated powers in a bill. It sets out some guiding principles and practical examples (which are not intended to be exhaustive).

The toolkit covers the following issues:

- What is the right balance between primary and secondary legislation?

- What is the proper role for delegated powers?

- Where will delegated powers not generally be justifiable?

- In what circumstances may it be appropriate to take powers that enable primary legislation to be amended (so called “Henry VIII powers”)?

- What alternatives should be considered when deciding whether to take a delegated power?

- What safeguards should be considered when it has been decided to take a delegated power?

Questions about the application of this guidance should be discussed in the first instance with departmental policy officials and lawyers, who can liaise with the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel and, as appropriate, with the Attorney General’s Office/Legal Secretariat to the Advocate General for Scotland for clarification or further assistance.

These issues will ultimately need to be resolved as part of the usual processes for agreeing the form and content of legislation before introduction, and with ministerial discussion where required.

This guidance is exclusively concerned with decisions about whether to take new powers in primary legislation. It is not intended to deal with the exercise of existing powers to make secondary legislation.

A. What is the right balance between primary and secondary legislation?

An Act of Parliament is the way that the most important aspects of policy are translated into law. An Act should contain the main aspects of a policy at an appropriate level of detail to be meaningfully scrutinised by Parliament, and to be understood and applied by those at whom it is aimed.

Delegated powers are generally used to give effect to the policy framework in the Act.

Example

The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 introduced marriage for same-sex couples in England and Wales. The Act allowed existing civil partnerships to be converted into a marriage. A delegated power was taken to allow ministers to set out how that procedure should work in practice (e.g. the information that should be provided to support an application).

As a rule of thumb, the more significant a legal change, the stronger the presumption that it should be set out in primary legislation so that it can be debated by Parliament via the bill process, rather than included within the scope of a delegated power.

B. What is the proper role for delegated powers?

Secondary legislation is an indispensable part of modern lawmaking, but it is vital that it is used appropriately, and not abused. The scope of powers, the rationale for their use, and whether any safeguards are appropriate (as below) should be properly tested and justified in every case.

Delegated powers are more likely to be appropriate for matters such as:

- dealing with secondary policy detail required to give effect to the Act, including technical or administrative matters (e.g. application processes, detailed procedural rules);

- making consequential changes to other legislation;

- including detail which may need amending more often than Parliament can be expected to legislate for by primary legislation, in circumstances where the purpose of the Act will be defeated if changes could only be achieved by further bills (e.g. in an area of rapidly evolving technology where references to technical concepts could quickly become defunct);

- dealing with things which can reasonably be anticipated to change regularly in the future (e.g. uprating sums in line with inflation);

- accommodating the fact that a detailed policy has to work differently for different groups of people, different areas, etc. (e.g. to set up a pilot scheme for a new policy in one part of the country) or has to deal with niche cases;

- dealing with emergency situations, where primary legislation is not feasible as a means of responding to fast-moving events (e.g. public health emergencies).

C. Where will delegated powers not generally be justifiable

Delegated powers should not generally be taken so as to make provision in future which is central to the effect of the Bill. That detail should normally be included on the face of a bill for scrutiny and debate as part of its passage.

For example, delegated powers should only exceptionally be taken to deal with:

- the creation or extension of generally applicable criminal offences or penalties (and regulatory offences, unless they are to be created by powers containing appropriate safeguards – see section F below);

- measures effecting significant constitutional change.

It is of particular importance that a delegated power which is capable of interfering with human rights is appropriately justified and contains proper safeguards (which may vary according to the nature of the right and the significance of the potential interference).

Delegated powers are unlikely to be appropriate, for example:

- to legislate for essential aspects of a policy framework which have not been set out in the Act (including ‘skeleton clauses’ which leave the real substance of the Act to regulations made under it);

- because there has been insufficient time for proper policy development; or where powers are being included speculatively on a ‘just in case’ basis.

D. In what circumstances may it be appropriate to take Henry VIII powers?

As a general rule, an Act of Parliament should be amended or repealed by another Act. Powers to amend or modify primary legislation by secondary legislation (sometimes called ‘Henry VIII’ powers) should only be taken where their necessity has been rigorously tested, and appropriate safeguards – or alternatives – fully considered.

Henry VIII powers are sometimes misunderstood as being unacceptable in all circumstances. What really matters, though, is the scope of the power, and the substance of the change that is capable of being made to primary legislation.

Some examples of where Henry VIII powers may be acceptable include:

- to amend detail which could well have been left to secondary legislation (see section B) but has been included in primary legislation to make the law easier for the reader to understand;

- to make consequential amendments to legislation in light of changes made by an Act;

- to add new cases to a legal framework set out in an Act, where not being able to do so would undermine the policy of that Act (e.g. in a policy environment involving rapid technological or other change, or where there is likelihood of abuse or avoidance).

Example 1

Section 339ZH(10) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 allows the Secretary of State to uprate in line with inflation the maximum penalty set out in the Act for failing to comply with a court order

Example 2

Section 10 of the Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Act 2023 allows the definition of ‘relevant animal’ in the Act to be updated in order to ensure consistency with related regulatory regimes.

By contrast, Henry VIII powers should not generally (and not without appropriate safeguards) be taken to amend the matters that are identified above as only exceptionally being the proper subject of a delegated power (see section C above).

The starting assumption is that Henry VIII powers should be subject to the affirmative procedure unless, having regard to the substance of the power, there is a good justification for a different level of scrutiny (e.g. because the power is only capable of making amendments of a minor character).

E. What alternatives should be considered when deciding whether to take a delegated power?

Some examples of alternative approaches to taking a delegated power may be:

- delaying introduction of the Bill until policy formulation is more advanced;

- including, on the face of the Bill, more aspects of the policy that a power seeks to implement;

- where policy formulation is still ongoing, to consider whether it may be possible and appropriate to proceed by way of Government amendment at a later stage.

F. What safeguards should be considered when it has been decided to take a delegated power?

Powers should be no wider than necessary to meet their intended objective. This is particularly important where the power is capable of amending primary legislation.

The wider a power, the more likely it is that specific safeguards should be included to uphold the proper constitutional balance between Parliament and the executive, and to guard against future abuse.

Some examples of appropriate safeguards, or alternative approaches, may include:

- express restrictions on the scope of a power (e.g. limiting to the expansion, rather than removal of rights granted by an Act; limiting its application to a particular group of people/type of case; setting statutory maximum limits on matters such as fines and sentences);

- a test or threshold that must be met, or process undertaken (e.g. consultation), before a power can be exercised;

- clear description of, or parameters around, what the power can positively do (e.g. describing as tightly as possible the kind of conduct that may amount to a regulatory offence);

- appropriate parliamentary scrutiny procedures: as a rule of thumb, powers capable of making more significant provision should be subject to the affirmative resolution procedure;

- sunset provisions (which mean that the power will expire, or must be renewed by Parliament, after a given period of time).

The implications of these different approaches will need to be carefully worked through, including by reference to legal and delivery risks.

Appendix G: Checklists for Each Stage

These checklists are not comprehensive and are not to be read in isolation but referred to alongside the relevant sections of the Guide. You should read all of the chapters on parliamentary stages in the Guide first to allow for timely preparation in advance of deadlines.

Preparing a Bill for Introduction

Before drafting legislation

Bid for the bill, completing a bid template provided by the PBL Secretariat.

Contact the PBL Secretariat to discuss the bid.

Obtain drafting authority from the Leader of the House of Commons for OPC to draft the bill.

Put in place resources: a bill team, legal team, and governance mechanisms.

If there is a joint bill team with two or more departments, agree a protocol for managing the bill.

Produce a clear delivery plan for developing the bill and supporting documents from now until after Royal Assent.

Arrange for training (contact the Parliamentary Capability team or the PBL Secretariat).

Engage the Union and Devolution Directorate, Territorial Offices and then the devolved governments on any devolved implications of the bill.

During drafting

Obtain collective agreement for the policy in the bill.

Work with departments across-government on any implications for their areas.

Contact the AGO and LSAG to discuss the key legal issues in the bill and whether any Law Officer consents will be required.

Consider the duty on Ministers of the Crown in section 19 of the Environment Act 2021 to have due regard to the environmental principles policy statement when making policy, including proposals that lead to legislation.

Contact the United Kingdom Intelligence Community to discuss whether the proposals impact on work of the Agencies.

Consider the impact, if any, on the Crown Dependencies and British overseas territories, as necessary, in consultation with MoJ and FCDO.

Contact the Data Protection Policy Team in DSIT to discuss whether the proposals which relate to the processing of personal data are compatible with data protection legislation.

Consult the Information Commissioner’s Office on any new data sharing proposals or gateways

Address any finance, public expenditure or tax implications of the bill and obtain the agreement of HM Treasury where necessary.

Seek Cabinet Office and HM Treasury ministerial approval before taking steps to establish, disestablish, re-classify, or merge an Arm’s-Length Body (ALB), if applicable.

Give the House Authorities an opportunity to comment on proposals intended to apply in relation to Parliament or the parliamentary estate.

Begin work on your economic and equalities impact assessments, if applicable.

Begin work on explanatory notes, delegated powers memorandum, ECHR memorandum, factsheets, “keeling schedules” and other supporting documents.

Keep in regular contact with the PBL Secretariat.

Before PBL Committee consideration of the bill for introduction

Ensure you have a plan to draft and deliver the documents required, and assigned members of the team. You will need to provide (see below for detailed checklists on each product):

- Bill print (OPC will provide)

- Explanatory Notes

- PBL Memorandum

- Parliamentary handling strategy

- Legal Issues Memorandum

- Delegated Powers Memorandum, if needed

- Impact Assessment and RPC opinion, if needed

Ask the PBL Secretariat for the templates.

Documents need to be circulated to PBL Secretariat one week before the Committee meeting, with drafts shared the week before that, or in the case of the Legal Issues Memo, at least three weeks before.

Ensure the AGO and LSAG are sent the draft legal issues memorandum three weeks before documents are sent to the PBL Committee. AGO and LSAG officials will need to comment on any draft requests for retrospection or early commencement in good time for the final requests to be sent to AGO and LSAG.

Explanatory Notes:

Identify the personnel who will be responsible for preparing the explanatory notes (ENs), including the person who will act as the point of contact with the Public Bill Offices (PBO).

Begin drafting the ENs (using the template), starting with the sections on policy background and legal background.

Seek comments from departmental lawyers throughout drafting of the Bill, including the final version of the ENs before they are sent to PBL Committee.

Consider whether you should consult OPC on parts of the ENs relating to territorial extent and application.

If the bill is to be introduced in the House of Commons, ask OPC to provide, or to clear, the wording for the part of the ENs that relate to parliamentary approval for financial costs or charges imposed.

Consult the Territorial Offices and Office of the Advocate General (as appropriate) to provide final clearance for the relevant sections of the notes.

Ensure the final draft of the ENs are consistent with the final text of the bill.

Arrange for the Public Bill Office to comment on the explanatory notes (at least two days before introduction).

Action any comments from the PBO.

Prepare a PBL Committee memorandum

Draft the Memo, summarising the content of the bill and any other important issues which have been covered in the other PBL Committee documents referenced above.

Proof read the final version of the Memo, ensuring all sections are complete.

Prepare a final parliamentary handling strategy

Draft the handling strategy.

Share the draft handling strategy with the Whips at least one week before they are submitted to the PBL Committee for circulation.

Action any comments to from the Government Whips’ Offices in the Commons and Lords.

Produce a delegated powers memorandum (DPM), if applicable, for publication

Draft the DPM, explaining the purpose of and justification for any delegation of power in the bill

Share the DPM with Lords Whips’ Office at least one week before they are submitted to the PBL Committee for circulation.

Action any comments from the Government Whips’ Office in the Lords.

Produce full impact assessment, if applicable

Engage with your departmental Better Regulation team.

Produce the impact assessment.

Engage with the RPC, where appropriate.

Action any comments from the RPC in relation to an initial opinion.

Draft the Legal Issues Memorandum (LIM)

Draft the LIM, setting out the justification for any provisions that may potentially be considered to touch on Convention rights in a legal issues memorandum. Consider the bill’s compatibility with the European Convention on Human Rights and arrange for the bill minister to sign the ECHR statement to support the bill.

Consider whether the bill contains environmental law (NB: the minister may need to sign a statement, or include a sentence in the ENs).

Consider whether the bill relates to Northern Ireland-Great Britain trade (NB: the minister may need to sign a statement, or include a sentence in the ENs)

Consider whether the bill is compatible with Scottish and Northern Ireland law. Consult with the Territorial Offices and Office of the Advocate General as appropriate in relation to any devolution matters.

Before PBL Committee

Clear the PBL Committee documents with your minister/s.

Submit the papers to PBL Secretariat one week before the PBL Committee meeting.

Brief your minister ahead of the PBL Committee meeting.

The House of Commons

Ahead of presentation/First Reading in the Commons

Arrange bill backers

If applicable, arrange for the minister to sign an ECHR statement.

Arrange for the minister to sign an environment law statement, or include a sentence in the ENs

Arrange for the minister to sign a Northern Ireland-Great Britain trade statement, or include a sentence in the ENs.

Agree that OPC can give notice of presentation of the bill.

Send the final bill print and ENs to the PBO (OPC will send the bill print; the bill team should send other documents including the ENs). The PBO will add the bill number and arrange printing of both documents.

Confirm with the Whips Office which minister will sit on the front bench to ‘nod’ in the bill.

If necessary, write to the devolved governments requesting their agreement to initiate the legislative consent process. You should repeat this whenever the bill is amended in a way which engages the legislative consent process.

On the day of introduction

Send the delegated powers memorandum to Commons PBO for publication (requires sending to the DPRRC when the Bill reaches the Lords - see Lords intro requirements).

Share soft copies with the PBO of: the impact assessment and Regulatory Policy Committee opinion (if applicable), ECHR memo (if separate analysis has been undertaken).

Send the ECHR memo to the JCHR.

Provide printed copies of relevant documents to the PBO, including:

- 50 copies of the delegated powers memo in the Commons Vote Office, and

- 50 copies of the impact assessment and Regulatory Policy Committee opinion (if applicable).

Arrange for publication on GOV.UK (on dedicated Bill page) of:

- Impact assessment(s) and Regulatory Policy Committee opinion (if applicable),

- Delegated powers memo and ECHR memo (if relevant), and

- Other supporting statements (e.g. fact sheets) where relevant.

Arrange for deposit of supporting documents in the House libraries.

After the bill has been introduced

Arrange for a written ministerial statement (WMS) to be issued (if relevant) and agreed with the Whips offices and No.10.

Send a ‘Dear Colleagues’ letter to MPs (as agreed with the Commons Whips office and No.10).

Send stakeholder and select committee correspondence (where relevant).

Issue a press notice and media briefings (where relevant).

Ahead of Commons Second Reading

Keep in touch with the Whips about the timing for Second Reading.

Meet the minister to understand their briefing requirements.

Arrange for ministers to open and close - agree the approach with the Whips Office.

Draft an opening speech, including details of the bill.

Draft a skeleton closing speech, with placeholders to respond to the expected areas of questioning, and rebuttals to any reasoned amendments tabled.

Provide a Q&A pack with top lines to respond to anticipated issues that will come up during the debate.

Take stock of stakeholder briefings and wider public narratives ahead of debate - and reflect positions in the briefing pack.

Ensure you have copies of speech for Hansard, and copies of the final briefing pack that can be annotated and passed to the minister (via the PPS) as necessary.

Agree officials to attend the box with the departmental parliamentary branch (establish a virtual box for policy leads/lawyers).

After Commons Second Reading

Provide a readout of the debate across the department, PBL Secretariat and business managers.

Follow up on any commitments e.g. ‘I will write’ letters.

Commons Committee Stage

Provide the Whips with a list of witnesses for oral evidence sessions (agreed by the bill minister).

With Whips and OPC, prepare programming resolution and standard motions for sitting in private and publication of written evidence.

Brief minister for programming sub-committee.

Prepare suggested questions for the minister to ask witnesses.

Develop a tracker for amendments.

Agree a process for responding to amendments and briefing ministers with policy, legal, press and private offices (including drafting / clearance processes). Communicate deadlines and expected pressure points to the department.

Arrange an early discussion with the Committee Clerk and agree process for the bill team to comment on draft groupings.

Consider providing a procedural brief on how Committee works to the bill minister (in discussion with the Whips office).

Draft clause/schedule stand part notes for each clause/schedule in the bill.

Agree suggested Government amendments needed with the PBL Secretariat and Whips offices before seeking collective agreement.

Seek collective agreement (PBL Committee and policy committee if needed)

Factor in time for instructing OPC to prepare any Government amendments.

Commission notes on amendments (explanations of amendments, speaking note and Q&A) to be cleared by legal and (if necessary) communications colleagues.

Stay in touch with the Whips offices about timing for Committee and what will be debated when.

Table Government amendments at least a week before consideration (having agreed that they can be tabled with the Whips); provide details in a letter to co-chairs of the Public Bill Committee (enclosing, as appropriate, supplementary delegated powers and ECHR memos).

If needed, discuss final grouping with the Clerk directly, or via OPC.

Provide final ministerial briefing pack.

Brief minister/s

Agree officials to attend the box and alert the departmental parliamentary branch. Establish a virtual box as required for those not attending in person.

During Committee: keep a list of Ministerial commitments and provide a readout of the debate across the department, PBL Secretariat and business managers.

Prepare script for minister at end of committee thanking co-chairs etc.

Ensure your explanatory notes are updated and ready to be re-published on Lords introduction

If applicable, ensure your Delegated Powers Memo is updated and ready to be published as soon as Committee Stage has concluded.

Keep in regular contact with the PBL Secretariat.

Commons Remaining stages(Report and Third Reading)

Keep in touch with the Whips office about the timing of remaining stages, including tabling deadlines and how the debate will run.

Obtain clearance for any Government amendments, factoring in time to instruct OPC to prepare any Government amendments that are wanted. Send a letter detailing amendments to the Official Opposition spokesperson (enclosing supplementary ECHR and delegated powers memos where appropriate).

Table amendments at least one week before the debate (having agreed that they can be tabled with the Whips).

Send a letter detailing amendments to the Official Opposition spokesperson (enclosing supplementary ECHR and delegated powers memos, where appropriate).

If necessary, issue further Dear Colleague letter covering key Government amendment and high-profile non-government amendments.

If you are at the final amending stage in the second House, ensure that any LCMs have been passed by the devolved legislatures.

Commission notes on amendments (explanations of amendments, speaking note and Q&A) to be cleared by legal and (if necessary) communications colleagues.

Agree with Whips terms of any supplementary programme motion.

If needed, discuss final grouping with the Clerk directly, or via OPC.

Provide a Q&A pack with top lines to respond to anticipated issues that could come up during the debate.

Brief minister.

Arrange any briefing sessions with MPs that may be required.

If the bill requires King’s and/or Prince’s consent, check that the Order Paper mentions this; if this has been omitted, it should be pointed out to OPC who will alert the House Authorities.

Arrange for a Minister, who is a privy counsellor, to signify Consent just before Third Reading, if applicable.

Ensure the Minister has a short Third Reading speech setting out how the bill has changed since introduction and thank Members for their interest in the bill.

Provide a readout of the debate across the department, PBL Secretariat and business managers.

Preparing to transfer to the second House

Ensure the ‘take up’ arrangements are clear (i.e. which Minister is to take charge of the bill in the second House).

Agree an approach to parliamentary engagement with the Whips Offices.

Ensure the bill, as amended in the Commons, is proof read and approved for publication.

Ensure explanatory notes are revised as necessary to publish alongside the bill. These needs to be cleared with the Public Bill Office in the Lords at least two to three working days before the bill is sent to the Lords.

Arrange a fresh ECHR statement to be signed.

If the Bill contains environmental law, arrange for the Lords Minister in charge of the Bill to sign an environmental law statement.

If the bill relates to Northern Ireland-Great Britain trade, arrange for the Lords Minister in charge of the Bill to sign a statement, or include a sentence in the ENs.

Revise and arrange for re-publication of the impact assessment(s) and delegated powers memorandum as necessary,

The House of Lords

Lords Introduction and First Reading

Note that after Third Reading in the Commons, the House copy of the print incorporating amendments (signed by the Clerk of the House) is delivered to the House of Lords with a message. There is no formal process for the Lords Minister to move First Reading (this will be done by the Whips.

If the bill starts in the Lords:

Agree that OPC can alert the PBO to the intention to introduce a bill (different to notice of presentation).

Ensure the government Peer is lined up to read the long title. If the bill started in the Commons, the Whip will read out the short title and formally move First Reading.

Send draft explanatory notes to the PBO for comment (at least two to three working days before introduction).

Arrange for the Lords Minister in charge of the Bill to sign an ECHR statement.

If the bill contains environmental law, arrange for the Lords Minister in charge of the Bill to sign an environmental law statement.

If the bill relates to Northern Ireland-Great Britain trade, arrange for the Lords Minister in charge of the bill to sign a statement, or include a sentence in the ENs.

Send the delegated powers memorandum to the DPRRC Committee.

Whether the bill starts in the Lords or Commons, departments also will need to:

Send final explanatory notes to the PBO the day before publication.

Share soft copies of the impact assessment(s), and ECHR memo (if separate analysis has been undertaken) with the Lords Publishing Team for publication on the Bill’s Parliament webpage.

Arrange for publication on GOV.UK (on dedicated Bill page) of:

- Impact assessment(s) and Regulatory Policy Committee opinion (if applicable),

- Delegated powers memo and ECHR memo (if relevant), and

- Other supporting statements (e.g. fact sheets) where relevant.

Make provision for revised editions of Acts ("keeling schedules") (where necessary).

Arrange press briefings and memos to be published after publication of the bill and supporting documents.

Set up necessary engagement with peers, either through an all-peers meeting or attending party group meetings.

Send any All Peers letters (as agreed with the Lords Whips office and No.10).

Lords Second Reading

Ahead of Second Reading, agree and arrange briefings for the lead Minister - usually the same Minister opens and closes.

Draft an opening speech.

Draft a skeleton closing speech and a briefing pack providing lines on issues that might come up.

Keep track of the Bill speakers list on the Government Whips’ Official website before the debate. The final list can be obtained from the Government Whips’ Office around lunchtime on the day of Second Reading (10am on Thursday).

Agree and arrange for officials to sit in the box including provision of passes.

During debate, provide any additional responses needed for the closing speech via notes to the Minister.

After the debate, respond to any outstanding questions or points via correspondence within 24 hours.

Update your parliamentary handling strategy based on what was raised during debate.

Lords Committee Stage

Stay in touch with the Whips offices about timing and what will be debated and when.

Consider providing a procedural brief on how Committee works to the bill Minister (in discussion with the Whips offices).

Design a system for tracking amendments and applying dummy numbers to ensure consistency.

Ensure any necessary Government amendments have been drafted, collectively agreed and tabled (having agreed that they can be tabled with the Whips) at least one week before Committee. Factor in time to instruct OPC to prepare these. Agree handling and communication of amendments being tabled with the Lords Whips office.

Send any supplementary delegated powers memo to DPRRC.

Agree a process for responding to amendments and briefing ministers with policy, legal, press and private offices (including drafting / clearance processes). Communicate deadlines and expected pressure points to the department.

Draft clause/Schedule stand part notes for each clause/Schedule in the bill.

Commission notes on amendments (explanations of amendments, speaking note and Q&A) to be cleared by legal and (if necessary) communications colleagues.

Provide the Whips office suggested groupings for debate.

Finalise the ministerial pack based on final groupings.

Brief the minister.

If needed, ensure your explanatory notes are updated as soon as Committee Stage has concluded, though republication at this stage is highly unusual (see 10.30).

Lords Report

Keep in touch with the Whips office about the timing, including tabling deadlines and how the debate will run.

Obtain clearance for any Government amendments or concessions in the usual way, factoring in time for OPC to prepare these and table before the deadline (having agreed that they can be tabled with the Whips). Agree handling and communication of amendments being tabled with the Lords Whips office.

Send any supplementary delegated powers memo to DPRRC.

Keep PBL Secretariat, No.10 and the Whips Offices regularly updated on risk areas (e.g. where there may be votes / defeats) and ensure there are processes for agreeing the approach to each amendment.

Draft notes on amendments to agreed drafting / clearance process.

Agree an approach to ministerial briefing and clearance of the approach.

If you are at the final amending stage in the second House, ensure that any LCMs have been passed by the devolved legislatures.

Respond to DPRRC, Constitution Committee and JCHR, if applicable.

Provide the Whips office a suggested grouping of amendments and update the Minister’s pack based on the final groupings (noting that Peers can change groupings on the day of debate).

Brief the minister.

If applicable, ensure your explanatory notes are updated and ready to be published as soon as Report Stage has concluded.

Lords Third Reading

Keep in touch with the Whips office about the timing, including tabling deadlines and how the debate will run.

Draft notes on any amendments tabled (note that the only amendments that are admissible are tidying up amendments and amendments to enable the Government to fulfil undertakings given at an earlier stage).

On tabling any Government amendments, send a letter to the Official Opposition spokespersons (attaching, as necessary, supplementary delegated powers and/or ECHR memos).

Send any supplementary delegated powers memo to DPRRC.

Ensure the Minister has a short speech for ‘Bill Do Now Pass’. It is customary to thank Members for their interest in the bill.

Prepare a statement for the minister to read before Third Reading commences to inform the House of the bill’s present LCM status where consent has not yet been received or has not been granted.

Brief the minister.

Ensure your explanatory notes are updated and ready to be published following Royal Assent.

If the bill started in the Lords, see: Preparing to transfer to the second House above for the checklist.

Ping-pong

Note: there are various complexities to ping-pong that cannot be captured in a checklist. This is therefore designed to give a sense of the issues to consider, but further detailed planning and training should be undertaken ahead of this stage.

Keep in touch with both Whips offices about the timing, including tabling deadlines and how the debate will run.

Arrange training for the bill team (the PBL Secretariat in consultation with OPC and the Whips Offices can support this).

Complete early analysis of issues that could be in play at ping-pong with options for responding.

Agree the approach to issues outlined above with the PBL Secretariat, No.10 and the Whips offices, and where necessary seeking contingent collective agreement from PBL Committee and the relevant policy committee to a range of options. This will enable speedy deployment if needed.

If necessary, ahead of Commons Consideration of Lords Amendments, issue further Dear Colleague letter covering key Government Lords amendments and non-government amendments.

Engage both MPs and peers ahead of ping-pong to ensure strong intelligence on the options and approach the House is likely to take (agree your strategy with the Whips Offices).

Agree the approach to all amendments and ensure OPC have the necessary instructions to draft the motions for debate, including reasons for seeking to overturn any amendments.

Prepare briefing for the Minister to respond to amendments during debate.

Ask the PBL Secretariat for the explanatory notes template used during ping-pong.

On return to the first House for the first time (only), submit explanatory notes on any amendments (government and non-government) made in the second House to the PBO.

In the Commons, it is for the bill minister to propose groupings for Lords amendments for debate. This should be done in consultation with the Whips Office.

If an amendment is overturned / rejected in the Commons, a Reasons Committee will meet to provide a reason for this. This is arranged by the Whips office, but the bill team will be asked to:

Input the reasons drafted by OPC; and

Confirm the name of the minister serving on the Committee.

Keep the master explanatory notes updated throughout ping pong as these will be needed once the bill reaches Royal Assent.

Royal Assent

Ensure the explanatory notes are updated to reflect any changes to the bill throughout the bill’s passage through the second House and during ping-pong.. They need to be in line with the Guide to Making Legislation (Note: no new template is needed; it is the original template with elements removed as set out in the Guide).

Ensure the Act and explanatory notes are proof-read before publication.

Send the final explanatory notes to Legislation Services at The National Archives for formatting and publication alongside the text of the Act.

Formally handover any work to the teams working on implementation e.g. any secondary legislation, guidance needed. Departments should highlight any debates that were pertinent to ongoing work to ensure this is factored into future handling

Conduct a lessons learned exercise (the PBL Secretariat or the Parliamentary Capability can support this).

Ensure all templates, documents and submissions are saved in shared areas for archive.

Share best practice and consider training for wider bill teams or within the department.

Arrange a celebration.

Private Members’ Bills

Ensure the department has a good system for tracking bills introduced by Members and for agreeing a position.

Ensure you are engaging with your legislative strategy team and/or parliamentary branch.

Taking a position on PMBs that have been introduced

Determine the policy and legislative implications, including the impact on the devolved governments, legal issues, compatibility with the European Convention of Human Rights, regulatory impact, and spending implications.

Ensure a clear ministerial decision is taken on whether to:

- Support the bill;

- Oppose the bill; or

- Remain neutral

If the Minister wishes to support the bill or take a neutral position, collective agreement must be sought. Engage with the PBL Secretariat as soon as possible to ask for bill document templates.

Attach to the write round:

- PBL memorandum

- Bill print

- Explanatory notes

- Legal issues memorandum (LIM)

- Parliamentary handling strategy,

- Delegated powers memo (if applicable)

- Impact assessment (if applicable).

Engage with OPC on drafting the bill print.

Contact the AGO and LSAG as soon as it is known that the Government may be supporting a PMB to ensure the LIM can be cleared.

Contact UDD to discuss any devolution implications.

Seek King’s and/or Prince’s consent, if applicable.

Ask the Member if OPC can hand in the bill and supporting documents.

If the Government wishes to make amendments to the bill, be clear in the write round what those amendments are.

If the Minister wishes to oppose the bill, write to PBL Committee for information ahead of Second Reading setting out the reasons why.

Government supported PMBs - after introduction

Support the Member as necessary (in consultation with the Whips offices).

Provide the minister with a briefing pack for all stages of the bill in the first House.

Ensure the impact assessment and delegated powers memo have been published and the latter shared with the Commons PBO for publication (requires sending to the DPRRC when the Bill reaches the Lords - see Lords intro requirements).

Ensure collective agreement is gained for any further amendments.

If any amendments are made to the bill, ensure the explanatory notes are updated to reflect the changes. If necessary, write to the devolved governments asking that they initiate the legislative consent process.

Ensure you have a good understanding of whether the relevant devolved governments are likely to secure a legislative consent motion before Report Stage in the first House.

Work with the Member to identify a MP/peer to pick up the bill in the second House.

Consider and set up systems to support the Member in the second House (in consultation with the Whips offices).

Send the delegated powers memorandum to the DPRRC Committee (cc’d to the PBO) when the bill passes to the second House.

Provide the minister with a briefing pack for all stages of the bill in the second House.

Arrange for a Minister, who is a privy counsellor, to signify Consent just before Third Reading, if applicable.

If the bill reaches Royal Assent, send the final explanatory notes to Legislation Services at The National Archives for formatting and publication alongside the text of the Act.

Government handout bills

Bid for the bill, completing a bid template provided by the PBL Secretariat.

Obtain drafting authority from the Leader of the House of Commons for OPC to draft the bill.

Obtain policy clearance for the content of the hand out bill ahead of the ballot.

Draft a ‘handout one pager’ setting out what the Bill does and share with the PBL Secretariat.

Agree a timetable to provide OPC with drafting instructions and provide them on time.

Ahead of the write round, engage with the PBL Secretariat and ask for the bill templates.

Attach to the write round:

- PBL memorandum

- Bill print

- Explanatory notes

- Legal issues memorandum (LIM)

- Parliamentary handling strategy,

- Delegated powers memo (if applicable)

- Impact assessment (if applicable).

Contact the AGO and LSAG as soon as it is known that the Government may be supporting a PMB to ensure the LIM can be cleared.

Contact UDD to discuss any devolution implications.

Seek King’s and/or Prince’s consent, if applicable.

Ask the Member if OPC can hand in the bill and supporting documents.

If a Member picks up the bill, consider and set up systems to support the Member (in consultation with the Whips offices).

Provide the minister with a briefing pack for all stages of the bill in the first House.

Ensure the impact assessment and delegated powers memo have been published and the latter shared with the DPRRC.

Ensure collective agreement is gained for any further amendments.

If any amendments are made to the bill, ensure the explanatory notes are updated to reflect the changes.

Ensure you have a good understanding of whether the relevant devolved governments are likely to secure a legislative consent motion before Report Stage in the first House.

Work with the Member to identify a MP/peer to pick up the bill in the second House.

Consider and set up systems to support the Member in the second House (in consultation with the Whips offices).

Send the delegated powers memorandum to the DPRRC Committee (cc’d to the PBO) when the bill passes to the second House.

Provide the minister with a briefing pack for all stages of the bill in the second House.

If the bill reaches Royal Assent, send the final explanatory notes to Legislation Services at The National Archives for formatting and publication alongside the text of the Act.
